terms.definition: The amount of matter in your body — the same number everywhere in the universe.
terms.function: Stays constant across all platforms; it is the 'stuff' of you, independent of any planet.
terms.whereItIs: The number on the mass/weight card that never changes as the astronaut hops platforms.
terms.whyItMatters: Confusing mass with weight is the most common gravity error — mass is a property of you, weight is a force between you and a world.

terms.definition: The force of gravity pulling on your mass — it changes with the world you're on.
terms.function: Determines the scale readout on each platform: mass × local gravity.
terms.whereItIs: The floating readout panel that updates as the astronaut moves from platform to platform.
terms.whyItMatters: Weight is why the same astronaut can feel light on the Moon and heavy on Jupiter.

terms.definition: How strongly a world pulls on objects at its surface, written as a multiple of Earth's (1 g).
terms.function: Sets the platform labels: Moon 0.17 g, Mars 0.38 g, Earth 1 g, Saturn 1.07 g, Jupiter 2.5 g.
terms.whereItIs: The label plane under each platform sphere in the row.
terms.whyItMatters: Surface gravity depends on both mass and radius — the two together explain every number in the row.

terms.definition: How much mass is packed into a given volume; Saturn is far less dense than Earth.
terms.function: Explains the Saturn surprise: low density plus a huge radius leaves surface gravity almost equal to Earth's.
terms.whereItIs: Referenced by the note tag on the Saturn platform.
terms.whyItMatters: Density is the missing ingredient that stops 'biggest = heaviest' from being true in space.

terms.definition: Earth's natural satellite, with surface gravity about one sixth of Earth's.
terms.function: Serves as the row's weakest-gravity reference — 0.17 g.
terms.whyItMatters: Apollo astronauts' famous bouncy moonwalk is pure gravity math: same mass, one sixth the weight.
